body.hook: In Alberta, the weather can change from sunny to snowing in an afternoon, and in winter, temperatures can fall below −30°C. Outdoor people have a saying: "There's no bad weather, only bad clothing." Knowing how to dress in layers keeps you warm, dry and safe.

vocabulary.definition: The layer next to the skin that moves sweat away.
The middle layer that traps body heat, such as fleece or wool.
The outer layer that blocks wind and water.

A dangerous drop in body temperature.

study.title: Dress for the Weather
study.question: How do I dress to stay safe and comfortable outdoors?
study.passage:
The three-layer system:
1. Base layer: wicks sweat away from skin. Synthetic fabrics or merino wool, not cotton.
2. Insulating layer: traps warm air. Fleece, wool or a down or synthetic jacket.
3. Shell layer: blocks wind, rain and snow.
Plus: a hat (much heat is lost from the head and neck), mitts or gloves, warm socks and waterproof boots.
Why not cotton? Cotton soaks up sweat and water and dries slowly, so it pulls heat away from the body. Outdoor educators say "cotton kills" in cold, wet conditions.
Warning signs:
• Frostbite: skin turns white or grey and feels numb or waxy, often on fingers, toes, ears and nose. Warm gently; don't rub.
• Hypothermia: shivering, clumsy hands, slurred speech, confusion. Get the person somewhere warm and dry and get help.
• Heat exhaustion (summer): heavy sweating, headache, dizziness. Move to shade, drink water.
Activity: Each group gets a weather card: (A) −15°C, wind 20 km/h, sunny; (B) 8°C, rain, windy; (C) 28°C, sunny, a 3-hour hike; (D) −2°C, wet snow. Choose clothing from a pile of real items (or picture cards) and explain each choice. Then go outside for 20 minutes and check how you feel.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; safety information summarized from Environment and Climate Change Canada and Alberta Health Services guidance.

body.hook: A sunny morning in the Rockies can turn into sleet by lunch. Experienced hikers never head out without a few key items, because when something goes wrong outdoors, what's in your pack is all you have.

vocabulary.definition: Items every outdoor traveller should carry, such as water, food, layers and first aid.
A small backpack for a one-day outing.
Finding your way, using a map, compass or GPS.
A light item such as an emergency blanket or bivy that protects from weather.
Drinking enough water to keep the body working well.

study.title: Pack Smart
study.question: What should I always bring outdoors, and why?
study.passage:
The outdoor essentials (a common list, written for this lesson):
1. Navigation: map, compass and a charged phone (phones can fail in cold or without signal).
2. Light: headlamp or flashlight with spare batteries.
3. Sun protection: sunglasses, sunscreen, hat.
4. First aid kit, including any personal medications.
5. Knife or multi-tool (for adult leaders on school trips; follow school rules).
6. Fire starter: matches or lighter in a waterproof bag (leaders carry, used only in emergencies or where allowed).
7. Emergency shelter: emergency blanket or bivy.
8. Extra food.
9. Extra water and a way to carry it.
10. Extra clothes: warm layer, rain jacket, toque and gloves, even in summer in the mountains.
Also: whistle (three blasts = help), garbage bag, ID and an emergency contact.
Activity: groups receive a pile of items, including some unnecessary ones (a hair dryer, a large speaker). Pack a day pack for a three-hour autumn walk in a nearby park, explain each choice, then weigh the pack.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; the essentials list follows common outdoor-safety practice.

body.objective: Students will be able to recognize and prevent cold and heat injuries.
body.iCan: I can recognize and prevent cold and heat injuries.
successCriteria: I can recognize signs of hypothermia, frostbite, heat exhaustion and heat stroke
I can explain how to prevent cold and heat injuries
I can describe basic first steps and when to get help
body.hook: In Alberta we can face −30 °C wind chills in January and +30 °C heat in July. Both can hurt you. Knowing the early signs of cold and heat injuries, and acting fast, keeps a fun day outside from becoming an emergency.

vocabulary.definition: A dangerous drop in body core temperature.
Freezing of skin and the tissue underneath.
An early, mild cold injury where skin turns pale and numb.
How cold it feels on exposed skin when wind is combined with temperature.
Overheating with heavy sweating, weakness, headache and nausea.
A medical emergency where the body overheats and can't cool itself.

study.title: Too Cold, Too Hot
study.question: How do I prevent and respond to cold and heat injuries?
study.passage:
Cold and heat guide (written for this lesson; summarizes common first-aid guidance; school first-aid procedures always apply):
Hypothermia: early signs: shivering, cold hands, clumsy movements, and the "umbles" (stumbles, mumbles, fumbles, grumbles). Prevent: layers, stay dry, eat and drink, keep moving. Respond: get to shelter, replace wet clothes, add layers, warm sweet drinks if alert; severe cases (shivering stops, confusion): call 911.
Frostnip and frostbite: skin turns white or greyish, feels numb or hard (cheeks, nose, ears, fingers). Prevent: cover skin, check each other's faces. Respond: warm gently with body heat; do not rub; get medical help for frostbite.
Wind chill: Environment and Climate Change Canada warns that at wind chills of about −28 and colder, exposed skin can freeze in 10–30 minutes.
Heat exhaustion: heavy sweating, pale clammy skin, dizziness, headache, nausea. Respond: move to shade, rest, drink water, cool with damp cloths.
Heat stroke: very high body temperature, confusion, may stop sweating, hot skin, fainting. This is an emergency: call 911 and cool the person right away.
Activity: scenario cards: groups identify the injury, the response and how it could have been prevented.
study.source: Summary written for this lesson; wind chill guidance from Environment and Climate Change Canada.
